Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 11 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 585 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

Draft:

Distance learning, the option to attend classes from home through online or video conferencing, is often dismissed as a poor substitute for the traditional classroom. I disagree. Students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home, because it gives them flexibility, protects their health and finances, and lets them learn in the way that suits them best. Schools should offer this option as a real choice, not a last resort.

The first benefit is flexibility. Many students have responsibilities that a fixed campus schedule cannot accommodate. A student who works part-time to pay tuition may not be able to commute across town for a nine o'clock lecture, and a parent caring for a young child may have no one to watch the baby during class hours. When a course can be joined from home, these students can keep their jobs and their families while still earning credit. Without that option, many of them would be forced to choose between education and everything else in their lives.

Second, attending from home can protect students' health and money. Commuting costs for gas, transit passes, parking, and campus meals add up quickly, especially for students who already live on tight budgets. During the influenza seasons and the pandemic years, many schools discovered that a student who could join class from bed while recovering from a cold did not have to fall behind or spread illness to classmates. Remote attendance turns an illness from a reason to miss a semester into a day of rest followed by a catch-up session online.

Third, learning from home suits many students' temperaments. Some students find it hard to speak up in a crowded lecture hall, but they become confident when they can type a question in a chat window or speak from a quiet room. Students with anxiety, disabilities, or sensory sensitivities may find a familiar home environment far easier to concentrate in than a noisy, unpredictable campus. Recorded lectures also let students pause, rewind, and review difficult material, something a single live lecture never allows.

Critics argue that students lose the social life of college, the spontaneous conversations, and the hands-on laboratory work that cannot be done through a screen. These concerns are valid, and they are the reason schools should not make distance learning the only option. A hybrid model solves most of the problem. Students who want the campus experience can attend in person, while those with good reasons to stay home can join remotely. Laboratory courses can keep their in-person sessions, and seminars can use video breakout rooms to keep discussion lively. The goal is to give students a choice rather than a single mandatory format.

Finally, the skills students build through remote learning are valuable in the modern workplace. Many employers now expect people to collaborate across time zones, communicate clearly in writing, and manage their own schedules. A student who has spent a semester organizing assignments, meeting deadlines without constant supervision, and participating in video discussions has practiced exactly these abilities. Far from being a lesser education, well-designed distance learning can prepare students for the way many people actually work.

In conclusion, students would benefit from attending classes from home. The option offers flexibility for working students and caregivers, lowers costs and protects health, and supports students who learn better in a familiar and comfortable setting. Schools that combine remote attendance with meaningful in-person opportunities give students the best of both worlds, and they treat them as adults capable of choosing how they learn.
